title: Generative AI Needs Adaptive Governance
extended_summary:
This paper argues that generative AI develops too quickly and across too many domains for traditional, static governance approaches to remain effective. The authors frame the central problem as a pacing mismatch: laws and regulatory processes are slow, while generative AI capabilities, deployment contexts, and associated risks evolve rapidly. They contend that one-and-done disclosure, registration, and risk-management regimes are prone to regulatory misalignment and may fail to address new harms as they emerge.

To address this, the paper proposes an adaptive AI governance framework inspired by adaptive governance in environmental policy and agile methods in software development. The framework expands the relevant actors beyond government, industry, and academia to include civil society and citizens, and organizes responsibilities into shared activities (share best practices, collaborate, use, monitor, inform, adapt) and actor-specific activities (financing, anticipating, challenging, training, innovating). The paper also gives examples of how adaptive governance could be operationalized, such as permanent government AI committees, structured review cycles, centralized incident repositories, and dedicated AI governance R&D funding.

The paper is conceptual rather than empirical and does not study a school, classroom, or educational intervention. Its conclusions are broad policy recommendations: AI governance should be iterative, monitored, transparent, and revisable over time, while still maintaining oversight and safeguards against regulatory capture, insufficient depth, and uncertainty. The authors also note that adaptive governance should account for both current harms and longer-term risks, and they suggest that AI literacy and education initiatives can support responsible public participation in governance.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI systems are AI models and chatbots that generate text and other content in response to prompts, including foundation-model-based assistants such as GPT-like systems.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper is a governance/theoretical discussion of generative AI broadly, using examples such as ChatGPT and Claude to motivate adaptive governance; it does not evaluate a specific instructional coaching or lesson-feedback tool.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a conceptual/governance paper with no empirical evaluation of an AI tool, no study design, and no outcome data. It proposes an adaptive governance framework rather than testing a tool in schools or coaching systems.
impact_tier_rationale: No instructional, educational, or school-implementation impact is measured. The paper discusses potential governance relevance only, so there is no reported effect on learner, teacher, or system outcomes.
